Rank features by information gain

Source: R/fs_infogain.R
fs_infogain.Rd

Scores every predictor by its information gain about the target, in bits, optionally divided by the predictor's own entropy to give a gain ratio. Accepts a single data frame or a list of data frames.

Usage

fs_infogain(
  data,
  target,
  numeric_bins = NULL,
  normalize = c("none", "gain_ratio"),
  top_n = NULL,
  remove_na = TRUE,
  verbose = FALSE
)

Arguments

data

A data frame, or a list of data frames that each contain target. A data.table is copied, never modified in place. Column names must be unique, non-empty, and not NA within each data frame, and list columns are not supported.

target

Name of the target column.

numeric_bins

Optional whole number of bins for numeric predictors and a numeric target, replacing the automatic count. Values below 2 are raised to 2. Default NULL (bins chosen per column).

normalize

"none" (default) for raw information gain in bits, or "gain_ratio" for gain divided by the predictor's split entropy. See "Cardinality bias and the gain ratio".

top_n

Optional whole number of at least 1. When supplied, selected holds the top_n highest-scoring features (fewer if fewer were scored). This is a rank cut, not a score floor, so a feature scoring 0 is selected if the ranking reaches it. When NULL (default), selected holds every feature with a score strictly greater than 0. A gain within floating-point rounding of zero, as an exactly independent predictor produces, is reported as exactly 0 and is not selected.

remove_na

If TRUE (default), rows with a missing target are removed first. See "Missing values" for why this rarely changes the result.

verbose

If TRUE, report how many features were scored, how many names occurred in more than one data frame, and how many were selected. Default FALSE.

Value

An fs_result object with:

selected

Selected feature names in decreasing order of score. A feature with an NA score is never selected.

scores

Named numeric vector of the score (gain or gain ratio) for every candidate feature, in decreasing order with NA last. For list input it covers the union of features across data frames, and a name found in several data frames keeps its highest score.

method

"infogain".

task

"classification", because the target is always treated as categorical.

model

NULL; no model is fitted.

details

A list with:

  • table: the full scored table, one row per scored column of each input, with columns Variable and InfoGain, plus SplitEntropy and GainRatio when normalize = "gain_ratio", plus Origin for list input.

  • normalize: the value used.

  • numeric_bins: the requested bin count as an integer, or NULL when automatic.

  • n_features: the number of distinct scored features, equal to length(scores).

  • collisions (list input only): the feature names found in more than one data frame, with Kept marking the row whose score was used. It has zero rows when no name repeats.

call

The matched call.

Details

Information gain is the drop in the entropy of the target once you know the value of one predictor: how many bits of uncertainty about the target that predictor removes. It makes no distributional assumptions and handles mixed column types, which makes it a cheap way to rank candidates before fitting any model.

It is a univariate filter. Each predictor is scored on its own, so two copies of the same information both score highly, and a predictor that matters only in combination with another scores low. Treat the ranking as a shortlist rather than a final feature set.

The default selection rule keeps every feature with a score above 0, which screens out almost nothing. On a finite sample, a predictor unrelated to the target still has a positive gain in almost every data set, and more so with more bins or levels. In a 200-row example with 50 pure-noise columns, all 50 are selected. Use top_n, or compare against gains computed on a permuted target, to make a real cut.

How columns are prepared

  • Numeric predictors are cut into equal-width bins. The number of bins is the larger of the Freedman-Diaconis and Sturges counts, at least 2, unless numeric_bins sets it. Under the automatic rule, a column with zero range or zero interquartile range gets 2 bins. A column with a single distinct value is one level either way and scores 0.

  • Character and logical predictors become factors.

  • Date and date-time predictors are replaced by three numeric columns, <name>_year, <name>_month, and <name>_day, which are then binned like any numeric column. If one of those names already exists in data, the call stops.

  • The target is always treated as categorical, so task is always "classification". A numeric target is binned by the same rule, once, on all rows where it is observed, so every predictor is scored against the same bins. A date target is treated as one class per day.

Missing values

Missing values are handled for each predictor-target pair separately: a missing value in one predictor does not remove that row for the others. A predictor with no complete pairs scores NA and is never selected.

remove_na has a narrow effect. Rows with a missing target are excluded pair by pair anyway, so the only difference shows when the target is entirely missing: remove_na = TRUE stops with an error, and remove_na = FALSE returns an NA score for every predictor.

Cardinality bias and the gain ratio

Raw information gain favors predictors with many distinct levels. A near-unique identifier column splits the data into groups of about one row, which drives the conditional entropy H(Y | X) to zero and gives it the largest gain any predictor can reach, H(Y), while carrying no signal that generalizes. Raw gains of predictors with different numbers of levels are therefore not comparable.

normalize = "gain_ratio" applies Quinlan's correction: each predictor's gain is divided by its split entropy H(X), the entropy of its (binned) level distribution. H(X) grows with the number of levels (it is log2(k) for k equally frequent levels), so the division penalizes a predictor for how finely it splits the data. A constant predictor has H(X) = 0 and gets a gain ratio of 0 instead of a division by zero. Gain ratios are on a different scale from raw gains, so do not reuse a threshold chosen for gains in bits.

See also

The Filter methods guide, which runs this function on a worked example.

Examples

# Single data.frame:
df <- data.frame(
  A = rep(1:10, each = 10),
  B = rep(c("yes", "no"), 50),
  when = as.Date("2020-01-01") + rep(0:24, 4),
  target = rep(1:2, 50)
)
res <- fs_infogain(df, target = "target")
res$selected
#> [1] "B"
res$scores
#>          B          A  when_year when_month   when_day 
#>          1          0          0          0          0 
res$details$table
#>     Variable InfoGain
#> 1          A        0
#> 2          B        1
#> 3  when_year        0
#> 4 when_month        0
#> 5   when_day        0

# Normalize by split entropy to offset the bias toward many-leveled
# predictors, and keep the two best-ranked features:
fs_infogain(df, target = "target", normalize = "gain_ratio", top_n = 2)
#> <fs_result> infogain (classification)
#> Selected 2 of 5 features
#>   B, A
#> Details: table, normalize, numeric_bins, n_features (in $details)

# List of data.frames:
df1 <- data.frame(A = rep(1:5, 20), target = rep(1:2, 50))
df2 <- data.frame(B = rep(c("yes", "no"), 50), target = rep(letters[1:2], 50))
fs_infogain(list(df1 = df1, df2 = df2), target = "target")
#> <fs_result> infogain (classification)
#> Selected 1 of 2 features
#>   B
#> Details: table, normalize, numeric_bins, n_features, collisions (in $details)
